prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of Romanian prose and poetry that builds an encyclopedic, metaphysical architecture from memory, the body and dream, with rare formal ambition and imaginative depth.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading my colleagues' arguments. Cărtărescu has an unmistakable voice: dense, patterned sentences carry a cosmology of memory, the body and dream. The Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid show formal ambition and imaginative and intellectual depth that do not depend on topicality or political symbolism. The shortlist entry and public knowledge place poetry at the origin of the prose and the large novels as the mature core, so the case rests on a whole authorship and not on one book. The long novels extend the project in scale and do not simply repeat the earlier work. Among the shortlisted writers, he combines singularity of voice, a sustained and coherent imaginative project and a depth that invites rereading. I treat this as a literary judgment about the work. The agreement among colleagues' openings is not evidence of merit and I do not rely on it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement is carried largely by Romanian syntax, rhythm and sonic patterning, so I cannot judge sentence-level quality through translation alone. A second reservation is that the very long, digressive late novels may reflect excess as much as purposeful pattern, and that point needs close reading across the whole corpus, not a general impression. Carson's hybrid forms and Wright's reconstruction of the novel are also serious achievements, and each is arguably less exposed to the translation problem in the form it takes in English.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Anne Carson first, arguing that she remakes the boundaries between classical scholarship, lyric, translation, essay and visual book design, and that her engagement with Greek and Latin sources is intellectually deep. He also notes that her case rests heavily on a few hybrid works and that her relation to the 'idealistic tendency' in Nobel's will is debatable.
responses.response: I agree that Carson's formal invention and intellectual depth are real, and I ranked her third for those reasons. I share the worry about concentration in a few books and about works whose effect depends on physical form. My assessment of Nox as an object also rests on public knowledge and not on handling it. The citation would have to say what counts as her authorship, given the weight of the translations and book-objects. I give more weight than you do to Cărtărescu's coherence across a large body of prose and poetry. I do not think the 'idealistic tendency' question separates the two cases, because it is open in both and neither oeuvre is topical in the way that question usually worries about.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a hallucinatory, richly patterned voice and a sustained metaphysical project. She also asks whether the density and length of the later novels are purposeful pattern or at times overextension, and she says coverage of the poetry and early stories is thinner than that of the large novels.
responses.response: I think that is the right question to put to the case, and I cannot settle it from translations. I would qualify it in one respect. The recurring images and obsessions, as you describe them, show that the length is part of a coherent method, so I read the risk as unevenness within books and not as lack of purpose. The thinner coverage of the poetry and early work is a gap I share, and the citation should be framed around the prose, with poetry named as the formative ground and not as an independently assessed body of work.

responses.point: Palm ranks Wright third, praising polyphonic novels that join political memory to mythic invention without reducing it to message. She also asks whether the oeuvre is yet large enough for the highest recognition and warns against reading it mainly through political symbolism.
responses.response: I agree that Carpentaria and The Swan Book are distinctive in scale and idiom, and that the merit has to be judged on narrative form and language. I also share your caution about letting the subject stand in for the assessment. I ranked Wright fifth in my opening because the small number of major novels makes sustained quality harder to judge. Your argument that each book is large and the later work extends the project moves me toward treating her as a closer alternative than I first did. Because of that, I list her among my alternatives. I still find the evidence for a deepening vision across a long career stronger for Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and cautions that the citation should not be narrowed to an 'Eastern European postmodern' label. She also notes that the poetry and early fiction are less known internationally, so corpus coverage in translation is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree on both points. A citation framed by region or movement would undersell a project that is better described through its own imaginative architecture of memory, body and dream. Your point about the poetry reinforces my own coverage caveat, so I would keep the proposed citation anchored in the prose and mention poetry cautiously.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's sentence-level density, rhythm and sonic patterning survives in English, French and other translations is unresolved, and I cannot verify it independently.
Coverage of the poetry and early fiction is incomplete in the supplied entry and in my own knowledge, so the claim of a coherent whole rests mainly on the large novels.
Whether the length and digression of the later novels is sustained pattern or overextension needs close reading of the whole corpus.

Carson's work depends partly on physical and visual form, and Wright's oeuvre is smaller in volume. I have not resolved how the 'significance across the body of work' criterion should weigh these differences.
I have not independently verified any source, and my views of the works rest on public knowledge and the supplied shortlist descriptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It lists no personal, professional or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist is context and not a reason for preferring a candidate.
